70.quote_or_event: “Would anyone have heard of Aristo and Gryllus except through Xenophon and Plato, their sons? Socrates keeps alive the memory of Sophroniscus.”
70.explanation: Arguing that a son can repay and even surpass what his father gave him, Seneca points out that many fathers are remembered only because of what their sons became, citing Agrippa’s obscure father alongside the fathers of Plato, Xenophon and Socrates.
70.tie_back: This is the Kural’s idea of a son’s service exactly: the child’s worth becomes the way the world comes to honour the parent.
70.source: Seneca, On Benefits (De Beneficiis), Book III, ch. 32 (tr. Aubrey Stewart)
70._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on Wikisource (On Benefits/Book III, Stewart). Seneca frames this as a son's benefit to his father that brings the father lasting fame, which is a close match to the Kural; the specific 'what penance did his father do' exclamation is not in Seneca.

79.quote_or_event: “For without friends no one would choose to live, though he had all other goods … for what is the use of such prosperity without the opportunity of beneficence, which is exercised chiefly and in its most laudable form towards friends?”
79.explanation: Opening his treatment of friendship (philia), Aristotle argues that wealth, office and power are worthless to someone with no bond of affection through which to use them.
79.tie_back: Like the Kural’s question of what use the outer limbs are without love, Aristotle asks what use the outer goods are without friendship, and the answer in both is: none.
79.source: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics, Book VIII, ch. 1 (1155a) (tr. W. D. Ross)
79._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim at MIT Internet Classics Archive (Ross). Strong structural parallel (what use are outward goods without inner affection), but Aristotle speaks of external goods and friendship, not bodily limbs and love as the body's inner organ.

84.quote_or_event: “Hospitality also is a theme of Theophrastus's praise, and rightly so. For, as it seems to me at least, it is most proper that the homes of distinguished men should be open to distinguished guests.”
84.explanation: Cicero commends hospitality as a fitting use of wealth and adds that, for those seeking honourable influence, generous entertainment of guests brings popularity and standing at home and abroad; he cites Cimon’s open-handedness as an example.
84.tie_back: Both texts treat the open, welcoming home as a source of good fortune for the host, though Valluvar stresses the glad face and casts the reward as Fortune herself taking up residence.
84.source: Cicero, De Officiis (On Duties), Book II, §64 (tr. Walter Miller (Loeb, 1913))
84._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on LacusCurtius (De Officiis II.44-89, Miller). Partial match: Cicero links hospitality to the host's benefit and influence, but he does not stress cheerfulness of countenance, and his benefit is social and political rather than prosperity as such.

91.quote_or_event: “Ninth, consider that a good disposition is invincible, if it be genuine, and not an affected smile and acting a part … And thou must do this neither with any double meaning nor in the way of reproach, but affectionately and without any rancour in thy soul.”
91.explanation: Among his rules for dealing with people who give offence, Marcus Aurelius says kindness only has power when it is real: speech must come from genuine affection and carry no hidden meaning or concealed ill-will.
91.tie_back: Valluvar’s sweet words are likewise defined by being steeped in affection and free of deceit, not by being pleasant on the surface.
91.source: Marcus Aurelius, Meditations, Book XI, §18 (ninth rule) (tr. George Long)
91._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim at MIT Internet Classics Archive (Long, Book XI). Strong match on affection without guile; the Kural's further point that such words come from people who have grasped what is right is only implicit in Marcus's Stoic context.

93.quote_or_event: “Such as a man's character is, he immediately shows it in his eyes, just as he who is beloved forthwith reads everything in the eyes of lovers … The good and simple and benevolent show all these things in the eyes, and there is no mistaking.”
93.explanation: Marcus Aurelius mocks the man who announces that he means to deal fairly, saying real goodness needs no announcement because it shows itself at once in a person’s eyes and bearing.
93.tie_back: The Kural likewise locates virtue in the welcoming face and kindly gaze, and treats these as outward signs of what is inside rather than as decoration.
93.source: Marcus Aurelius, Meditations, Book XI, §15 (tr. George Long)
93._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim at MIT Internet Classics Archive (Long, Book XI). Close on the face and eyes showing inner goodness; Marcus does not mention sweet speech, which is the Kural's third element.

172.quote_or_event: “Now, suppose a wise man had just such a ring, he would not imagine that he was free to do wrongly any more than if he did not have it; for good men aim to secure not secrecy but the right.”
172.explanation: Retelling Plato’s story of Gyges’ ring of invisibility, Cicero argues that a good person would not use a guarantee of impunity to take what is not his, because what restrains him is the wrongness of the act and not fear of being found out.
172.tie_back: This matches the Kural’s inner safeguard: the person who is ashamed of injustice turns down disgraceful gain even when nothing outside him would stop him.
172.source: Cicero, De Officiis (On Duties), Book III, §38 (tr. Walter Miller (Loeb, 1913))
172._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on LacusCurtius (De Officiis III.35-95, Miller). Strong match on restraint grounded in internal moral sense rather than fear of consequences; Cicero speaks of a commitment to the right rather than naming shame (naan) specifically.

174.quote_or_event: “Not even the impudence of my accusers dares to say that I have ever exacted or sought pay of anyone; they have no witness of that. And I have a witness of the truth of what I say; my poverty is a sufficient witness.”
174.explanation: At his trial Socrates points to his own poverty as proof that, despite years of teaching, he never took money from anyone, and he had earlier said he lived in utter poverty because of his devotion to the god.
174.tie_back: Socrates is the Kural’s person of clear vision who stays poor but does not reach for what is not his.
174._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim at MIT Internet Classics Archive (Jowett). Strong example of integrity kept in poverty; the parallel is to refusing fees rather than to coveting another person's property, and the Kural's sense-mastery theme is absent. Quote begins mid-sentence ('...but now, as you will perceive, not even...'); the capital 'N' is editorial.

181.quote_or_event: “We may, however, enter, though sparingly, into discourse sometimes when occasion calls for it, but not on any of the common subjects … but principally not of men, so as either to blame, or praise, or make comparisons.”
181.explanation: In his rules for everyday conduct, Epictetus tells the student that talking about other people, and above all finding fault with them, is the first kind of conversation to give up.
181.tie_back: Valluvar picks out the same habit as the one to drop first, so much so that someone who manages only this much has still done something good.
181.source: Epictetus, Enchiridion, ch. 33 (tr. Elizabeth Carter (as edited at the Internet Classics Archive))
181._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim at MIT Internet Classics Archive (Carter). Strong on refraining from blaming people in speech; Epictetus does not single out speaking behind someone's back, nor make the Kural's 'at least he does this' concession.

182.quote_or_event: “But of all forms of injustice, none is more flagrant than that of the hypocrite who, at the very moment when he is most false, makes it his business to appear virtuous.”
182.explanation: Having said that wrong is done either by force or by fraud and that fraud is the more contemptible, Cicero ranks the hypocrite who wears a mask of goodness while deceiving as the worst wrongdoer of all.
182.tie_back: Like Valluvar, Cicero says the false friendly face is worse than open wrongdoing.
182.source: Cicero, De Officiis (On Duties), Book I, §41 (tr. Walter Miller (Loeb, 1913))
182._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on LacusCurtius (De Officiis I.20-41, Miller). Very close on the ranking (hypocrisy worse than open wrong); Cicero speaks of hypocrisy generally rather than slander behind someone's back specifically.

190.quote_or_event: “We have other men's vices before our eyes, and our own behind our backs.”
190.explanation: Seneca says anger at other people grows from this lopsided vision, and gives the example of a father, worse than his son, who scolds the son for the very extravagance he once indulged in himself.
190.tie_back: Seneca names the same blindness as the Kural, and like Valluvar treats it as the root of the harm people do to one another.
190.source: Seneca, Of Anger (De Ira), Book II, ch. 28 (tr. Aubrey Stewart)
190._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on Wikisource (Of Anger/Book II, Stewart). Near one-to-one match on the image and its moral consequence. Same idea as the Aesop fable in the Greek mythology slot, but from a separate philosophical source.

246.quote_or_event: “And, generally, we feel pity whenever we are in the condition of remembering that similar misfortunes have happened to us or ours, or expecting them to happen in the future.”
246.explanation: In his analysis of the emotions, Aristotle says pity depends on remembering or expecting suffering of one’s own, so those who think themselves beyond harm feel little of it.
246.tie_back: This gives the psychology behind the Kural’s charge: those who drop compassion have forgotten what they themselves have suffered.
246.source: Aristotle, Rhetoric, Book II, ch. 8 (1386a) (tr. W. Rhys Roberts)
246._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim at MIT Internet Classics Archive (Roberts). Strong on the link between remembering one's own suffering and compassion; Aristotle describes how pity works and does not condemn its loss or speak of losing life's true purpose.

381.quote_or_event: “First, there must be food; secondly, arts, for life requires many instruments; thirdly, there must be arms … fourthly, there must be a certain amount of revenue, both for internal needs, and for the purposes of war; fifthly, or rather first, there must be a care of religion … sixthly, and most necessary of all …”
381.explanation: Setting out what a state cannot exist without, Aristotle lists six requisites, among them food, arms, revenue and, last and most necessary, a power of deciding what is just and expedient among citizens.
381.tie_back: Like Valluvar’s six limbs of the state, Aristotle’s list gives six things a polity must have, including the army and the treasury, though the two lists differ item by item.
381.source: Aristotle, Politics, Book VII, ch. 8 (1328b) (tr. Benjamin Jowett)
381._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim at MIT Internet Classics Archive (Jowett, Book VII). Striking six-fold structure with overlaps (arms/army, revenue/resources); Aristotle's arts, religion and judiciary do not match the Kural's ministers, allies and forts, and there is no lion simile. The sixth item is summarised in the explanation, not quoted.

386.quote_or_event: “A readiness to listen to those who had anything to propose for the common weal … He was also easy in conversation, and he made himself agreeable without any offensive affectation … There was in him nothing harsh, nor implacable, nor violent.”
386.explanation: Marcus Aurelius describes his adoptive father, the emperor Antoninus Pius, as a ruler who listened to anyone with something useful to propose, was easy to talk to, and had nothing harsh about him.
386.tie_back: This is the Kural’s praiseworthy king drawn from life: easy to approach and never harsh in speech.
386.source: Marcus Aurelius, Meditations, Book I, §16 (tr. George Long)
386._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim at MIT Internet Classics Archive (Long, Book I); excerpts joined with ellipses from the long §16 portrait. Strong match on accessibility and absence of harshness; the Kural's result (the world praising his land) is not stated here.

387.quote_or_event: “It is not easy to say how far an affable and courteous manner in conversation may go toward winning the affections.”
387.explanation: Cicero tells his son that a courteous, kindly manner of speech wins people over in ways that are hard to measure, and points to letters from Philip, Antipater and Antigonus urging their heirs to win the people with kind words.
387.tie_back: The Kural likewise says the ruler who gives with kind words finds the world following him, though Cicero stresses gracious speech more than giving and protection.
387.source: Cicero, De Officiis (On Duties), Book II, §48 (tr. Walter Miller (Loeb, 1913))
387._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on LacusCurtius (De Officiis II.44-89, Miller); the quote begins mid-sentence ('...and yet, it is not easy to say...'), with an editorial capital 'I'. Partial match: covers kind words winning affection, but not the Kural's pairing with generosity and protection of those who come to the ruler. The content of the royal letters is summarised from the surrounding passage.

university.172: Where kural 171 threatened consequences, 172 names the internal safeguard: நாண் (naan), a moral sense of shame or modesty, here specifically shame at நடுவன்மை (naduvanmai, “non-equity”). The phrase படுபயன் (padupayan) denotes the gain that “falls” to one, the benefit that would accrue from taking another’s property, and பழிப்படுவ (pazhippaduva) are acts that incur public blame. Valluvar’s psychology is notable: the person of integrity is restrained less by fear of punishment than by an internalised aversion to injustice, a theme developed fully in chapter 102 (நாணுடைமை). This aligns with Gita ethics, in which modesty (Sanskrit hri) and the reflex of weighing gain against righteousness are marks of a mature moral agent.
university.174: This kural removes the most sympathetic excuse for covetousness: need. இலம் என்று (ilam endru, “saying ‘we have nothing’”) captures the self-justifying thought of the poor, and Valluvar insists that even this does not license desire for another’s goods among those who are புலம் வென்ற (pulam venra, “sense-conquered”) and of புன்மையில் காட்சி (punmaiyil kaatchi, “vision free from meanness”). The pairing of sense-mastery with non-covetousness is characteristically Indian (compare the Gita’s sthitaprajna), but the insistence that integrity must survive poverty is universal, as Agur’s prayer in Proverbs attests. Valluvar is not romanticising poverty; he is arguing that virtue that fails under pressure was never virtue.
university.316: This is Valluvar’s clearest statement of the negative Golden Rule, and it is regularly cited alongside Hillel and the Mahabharata in comparative discussions of that principle. The phrase thaan unarndhavai, ‘what one has oneself felt or known,’ grounds the rule in lived experience rather than abstract principle: each person’s own suffering is a textbook of what not to do. Thunnaamai (not approaching, not engaging in) makes the prohibition wide enough to cover even drawing near to such acts. Unlike the positive form (‘do unto others’), the negative form sets a minimum that anyone can meet, and so needs no guesswork about what others want. It closely matches Brihaspati’s summary of dharma in the Mahabharata, Hillel’s one-sentence Torah, and Isocrates’ advice to the Cyprians.
